intro: Excerpts copied from the live Naya source (C:\APPS\NAYA). Each shows the real code behind a capability and explains what it does. Naya reuses Maia's engine via a DB-redirect shim, runs an 8-model failover chain from the database, routes by LLM-extracted intent, and gates every filesystem action behind explicit approval.

snippets.title: Repoint Maia's engine at Naya's database
snippets.feature: Sibling-of-Maia: reuse Maia's code, keep separate data
snippets.code:
import maia_db as _mdb

# ── Redirect ALL database operations to Naya's own file ──
_mdb.DB_FILE = os.path.join(r"C:\APPS\NAYA", "naya.db")

# Re-export every public symbol so callers can use `import naya_db as db`
# and get identical function signatures — all backed by C:\APPS\NAYA\naya.db
from maia_db import *          # noqa: F401, F403
from maia_db import _conn      # re-export private connection helper too
snippets.explanation: This three-line trick is what makes Naya a sibling of Maia rather than a fork. It imports Maia's maia_db module, overwrites its DB_FILE attribute to point at C:\APPS\NAYA\naya.db, then re-exports every function. Every downstream module (maia_context, maia_lang, naya_server) that does `import naya_db as db` now runs Maia's proven code against Naya's own data — no duplication, no cross-contamination with maia.db.

snippets.title: Import order matters — patch before maia_* loads
snippets.code:
NAYA_HOME = r"C:\APPS\NAYA"
QI_PATH   = r"C:\APPS\QI"
sys.path.insert(0, QI_PATH)
sys.path.insert(0, NAYA_HOME)

# naya_db MUST be imported first — it patches maia_db.DB_FILE to C:\APPS\NAYA\naya.db
# so all subsequent maia_* imports (rag, lang, context) transparently use naya.db
import naya_db as db

import maia_lang as _maia_lang
import maia_context as ctx_builder
snippets.explanation: The patch only works if it lands before any other module imports maia_db. naya_server puts both C:\APPS\NAYA and C:\APPS\QI on the path, imports naya_db first to apply the DB redirect, and only then imports maia_lang and maia_context — which now resolve to Naya's database. Get the order wrong and Maia's modules would silently read maia.db.

snippets.title: The /ask endpoint
snippets.explanation: Every conversation — from the Gradio console and from Telegram — funnels through this one Flask route. It defaults the conversation key to a per-day bucket, delegates all the real work to ask_naya(), then persists both the user message and Naya's reply to the conversations table (via the patched db.save_message). Telegram and the File Manager reuse the same ask_naya()/dispatch path so behaviour is identical across surfaces.

snippets.title: Telegram long-poll (no inbound port)
snippets.explanation: Naya's only chat channel is Telegram, and it works by OUTBOUND long-polling: a daemon thread repeatedly calls getUpdates with a 30-second hold and tracks the update offset. Because Naya reaches out to Telegram rather than receiving a webhook, no inbound port is ever opened — which is exactly why the registry can keep Naya strictly LAN-only. Replies are further restricted to authorised chat IDs (naya.telegram_allowed_chat_ids).

snippets.title: Walk the chain, fall over on failure
snippets.explanation: Naya's intelligence is config-driven: get_bot_llm_chain reads the llm_chain rows from naya.db in priority order, and the loop tries each active model until one returns. force_fast reorders to cheap local models for intent extraction; force_sonnet promotes Claude for hard questions when anthropic_mode is 'fallback'. The live chain is DeepSeek-R1 8B (primary, local) -> Cloudflare Qwen -> GPT-OSS 20B local -> Gemma3:27b -> Qwen3:4b -> MiniMax M2.5 -> GPT-OSS 120B -> Claude Sonnet.

snippets.title: Per-provider call branches
snippets.feature: One chain, three transport styles (Anthropic / Ollama / OpenAI-compatible)
snippets.explanation: Each chain entry names a provider, and _llm_call dispatches to the matching transport: the Anthropic SDK for Claude, Ollama's local OpenAI-compatible endpoint at 127.0.0.1:11434 for free local models, and a generic OpenAI-compatible POST (with a bearer key) for OpenRouter and Cloudflare. Because they all share the same messages shape, adding or reordering a model is a database edit, not a code change.

snippets.title: Optional escalation to NEXUS multi-AI synthesis
snippets.feature: Route hard questions to many AIs at once
snippets.explanation: For complex questions Naya can defer to the sibling NEXUS project, which fans the prompt out to many AIs and merges the best answer. It is opt-in (personal.nexus_enabled must be 'true') and fails closed — any error or ok=false returns None so ask_naya simply falls through to Naya's own local chain. The appended note tells the owner how many models contributed.

snippets.title: LLM-first intent schema
snippets.feature: Classify every message into a structured action
snippets.code:
ACTIONS = {
    "scan_index":      "Scan and index ALL files in a directory or drive",
    "scan_duplicates": "Find exact duplicate files (same content, SHA256 hash)",
    "scan_similar":    "Find similar files (fuzzy filename matching, near-duplicates)",
    "show_results":    "Show results of the most recent scan",
    "find_largest":    "Find the largest files consuming the most disk space",
    "delete_dupes":    "Delete duplicate files — keeps one copy (requires approval)",
    "generate_report": "Generate a storage or duplicate report as PDF/Word/Markdown/text",
    "schedule_task":   "Schedule an action to run at a future or recurring time",
    "undo":            "Undo the last file operation (restore deleted/moved files)",
    "drive_usage":     "Show disk drive usage statistics and free space",
    "general":         "General conversation or anything NOT file-management",
    # ... ~25 actions total
}
snippets.explanation: Instead of brittle keyword matching, Naya sends every message to the LLM with this action vocabulary and asks for a single JSON intent object. The model returns {action, target, destination, format, schedule_time, chain_action, confidence}. 'general' is the escape hatch — it means 'this is just a question, answer it normally'. This is the PRIMARY router; the old keyword matcher is now only a fallback.

snippets.title: Dispatch an intent to its handler (with chaining)
snippets.feature: Action dispatcher shared by chat, Telegram and the UI
snippets.code:
action = intent.get("action", "general")
if action == "general":
    return None  # Let LLM handle it

handler = _HANDLERS.get(action)
if not handler:
    return None

intent["conv_key"] = conv_key
result = handler(intent, conv_key)

# Compound chaining — if LLM detected two actions in one message
chain_action = intent.get("chain_action", "").strip()
if chain_action and chain_action != action:
    chain_handler = _HANDLERS.get(chain_action)
    if chain_handler:
        chain_intent = dict(intent)
        chain_intent["action"] = chain_action
        chain_intent["target"] = intent.get("chain_target", "")
        chain_result = chain_handler(chain_intent, conv_key)
        if chain_result:
            result = result + "\n\n---\n\n" + chain_result
return result
snippets.explanation: dispatch() turns a parsed intent into action. 'general' returns None so the caller falls through to the free-form LLM. Otherwise it looks the action up in _HANDLERS and runs it. If the model split a request like 'reset the dashboard and scan F:' into action + chain_action, both handlers run and their outputs are concatenated. The same _HANDLERS table backs chat, Telegram, and the Gradio File Manager (via dispatch_action).

snippets.title: Streaming SHA-256 that never crashes a scan
snippets.explanation: Hashing is how Naya proves two files are byte-for-byte identical. It reads in 64KB chunks so even multi-gigabyte files don't blow up memory, and it swallows every read error to return None — a locked or permission-denied file is skipped, never fatal. Over many scans this has populated ~2.7M similarity-group rows in naya_brain.db.

snippets.title: Four-phase duplicate detection
snippets.feature: Hash only what could possibly collide
snippets.explanation: The clever part of the scanner: hashing is expensive, so Naya never hashes a file that can't have a twin. Phase 1 walks the drive (skipping system dirs and tiny files), Phase 2 buckets by exact byte size, and only files that share a size with another get hashed in Phase 3. Phase 4 keeps groups of 2+. The loop checks _is_scan_cancelled between files so a long scan can be stopped from chat ('kill scan').

snippets.title: Persist groups with reclaimable bytes
snippets.feature: Record duplicates and how much space they waste
snippets.code:
for h, files in dup_groups.items():
    paths = [f[0] for f in files]
    sizes = [f[1] for f in files]
    wasted = sum(sizes) - min(sizes)  # bytes freed if keeping 1 copy
    total_wasted += wasted
    conn.execute(
        """INSERT INTO naya_similarity_groups
           (scan_id, group_type, file_hash, file_count, wasted_bytes,
            file_paths, file_sizes, status, created_at)
           VALUES (?, 'exact', ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, 'open', ?)""",
        (scan_id, h, len(paths), wasted,
         json.dumps(paths), json.dumps(sizes), datetime.now().isoformat()))
snippets.explanation: Each duplicate group is stored as one row in naya_similarity_groups, with the member paths/sizes serialised as JSON and wasted_bytes computed as 'total size minus one copy' — the space you'd reclaim by keeping a single file. The scan summary later orders open groups by wasted_bytes so chat answers and the Naya Brain tab lead with the biggest wins.

snippets.title: Whole-system storage analysis
snippets.code:
drives = get_drive_status()
candidates = []

# Phase 1: Quick scans (Windows temp, browser caches, app caches, recycle bin)
candidates.extend(scan_temp_locations())
candidates.extend(scan_browser_caches())
candidates.extend(scan_app_caches())
candidates.extend(scan_recycle_bin())

# Phase 2: FileHQ index queries (no filesystem walk needed)
if (dupes := get_filehq_dupes_summary()):
    candidates.append(dupes)
if (old_large := get_filehq_old_large_files()):
    candidates.append(old_large)

candidates.sort(key=lambda c: c["size_bytes"], reverse=True)
total_savings_mb = sum(c["size_mb"] for c in candidates)
snippets.explanation: The advisor combines two data sources: fast filesystem scans of the usual junk locations (temp, caches, recycle bin) and zero-walk queries against the FileHQ index for duplicates and old-large files. Everything is normalised into ranked cleanup 'candidates' sorted biggest-first, with a running total of potential savings — the basis for the plan it then proposes and (on approval) executes.

snippets.title: Read-only folder insight, cached
snippets.feature: Summarise any folder from the FileHQ index
snippets.code:
# Check cache first (unless refresh requested)
if not refresh:
    row = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM naya_folder_insights WHERE folder_path=?",
                       (path,)).fetchone()
    if row:
        generated = datetime.fromisoformat(row["generated_at"])
        if datetime.now() - generated < timedelta(hours=24):
            return dict(row)

# Query FileHQ for files under this path (read-only)
fhq = _filehq_conn()
rows = fhq.execute("""
    SELECT path, filename, extension, size_bytes, modified_date, category, archive_era
    FROM files
    WHERE (path LIKE ? OR path = ?) AND status = 'indexed'
""", (path + "\\%", path)).fetchall()
snippets.explanation: When asked 'what's in folder X?', memory first checks naya_folder_insights for a result less than 24 hours old, and only otherwise queries the FileHQ index — opened read-only (file:...?mode=ro) so insight gathering can never modify the file catalogue. The aggregated counts, sizes, dominant types and age range are then cached back for next time.

snippets.title: Approval gate on every destructive action
snippets.explanation: Every handler that could move or delete files calls _is_approved() against a boolean flag in naya.db (e.g. personal.file_modify_approved, which defaults to false). If it isn't set, the handler returns _perm_denied(), which tells the owner the exact phrase to say to grant permission. Approval is a deliberate, spoken act — Naya never flips these flags on its own.

snippets.title: Permission and folder-access commands run first
snippets.feature: Owner can grant/revoke before any action is attempted
snippets.code:
# ─── File Permission Approvals — MUST run before intent router ───
# "approve run commands", "approve delete", "revoke all", "show permissions"
# The router would intercept "approve run commands" as verb=run and fail the gate.
_perm_resp = _try_permission_command(message)
if _perm_resp:
    return _perm_resp

# ─── Folder Access Control — "add X as exception" / "protect X" ───
_access_resp = _try_folder_access_command(message)
if _access_resp:
    return _access_resp
snippets.explanation: Order is a safety feature. Approval and folder-protection phrases are intercepted at the very top of the turn pipeline, before the intent router runs — otherwise 'approve run commands' would be misread as a run action and bounce off the very gate the owner is trying to open. Protected folders and exceptions are tracked per-path in naya_folder_access.

snippets.title: Carry messages between sibling bots Telegram won't connect
snippets.feature: Tasuke / Maia / Naya conversation over HTTP
snippets.explanation: Telegram refuses to deliver messages from one bot to another, so sibling QI bots that share a chat talk over an HMAC-signed HTTP bridge instead. Naya loads the shared-chat roster and the signing secret from either the Windows path or the WSL/OpenClaw mirror, so the bridge works whether the peer lives on Windows or inside WSL. The /webhook/peer-bridge route verifies the signature before accepting a relayed message.

snippets.title: Scan + similarity-group schema
snippets.feature: Where every duplicate group is stored
snippets.code:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS naya_similarity_groups (
    id           INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    scan_id      TEXT NOT NULL,
    group_type   TEXT NOT NULL,          -- 'exact' | 'fuzzy_name'
    file_hash    TEXT,
    file_count   INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    wasted_bytes INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    file_paths   TEXT NOT NULL,          -- JSON array
    file_sizes   TEXT,                   -- JSON array
    status       TEXT DEFAULT 'open',    -- open | resolved
    created_at   TEXT NOT NULL,
    FOREIGN KEY (scan_id) REFERENCES naya_scans(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_sim_type ON naya_similarity_groups(group_type, status);
snippets.explanation: The file-intelligence brain lives in naya_brain.db, separate from the conversational naya.db so a giant scan history never bloats chat. naya_similarity_groups is its biggest table (~2.7M rows): each row is one duplicate or near-duplicate group, with member paths/sizes as JSON, the reclaimable wasted_bytes, and a status the executor flips to 'resolved'. The FK to naya_scans with ON DELETE CASCADE means clearing a scan removes its groups too.

snippets.title: Mark groups resolved after cleanup
snippets.feature: Close out duplicates once acted on
snippets.code:
placeholders = ",".join("?" for _ in group_ids)
conn.execute(
    f"UPDATE naya_similarity_groups SET status='resolved' WHERE id IN ({placeholders})",
    group_ids)
snippets.explanation: After the executor has deleted or kept a duplicate group, the scanner flips its status from 'open' to 'resolved' so it stops showing up in summaries and dashboards. Combined with the 'reset_dashboard' action (which sweeps completed/cancelled scans), this is how the 2.3 GB brain store is meant to be kept manageable over time.
